stories.headline: Alexander Isak kickstarts Liverpool career after 'difficult' start
stories.summary: Alexander Isak said his difficult start to his Liverpool career is now behind him after he scored a brace inside nine minutes to inspire his side to a 2-0 win at Ipswich on Friday.
stories.body:
Alexander Isak said his difficult start to his Liverpool career is now behind him after scoring a brace inside nine minutes to inspire his side to a 2-0 win at Ipswich on Friday.

Following his British-record £125 million ($170m) move from Newcastle United, Isak endured an injury-hit debut campaign at Anfield in which he scored only four goals in 22 appearances.

- Alexander Isak gives Andoni Iraola first Liverpool win as Bradley Barcola debuts

- Liverpool ratings: With 9/10 performance, is Isak's big breakout coming?

- Ranked: Top 50 most expensive Premier League transfers this summer, by true cost

But his double at Portman Road took the 26-year-old up to three goals in three Premier League games this campaign.

"It was not easy. It was a long injury, a difficult season in general," the Sweden striker told Sky Sports "I was thinking: I want to have a good World Cup firstly and then to start the season well, which I feel like I've done now.

"That season is kind of behind me, but it wasn't easy."

Isak's goals gave Andoni Iraola his first win as Liverpool boss at the third time of asking. And the former Bournemouth coach said after that he has no concerns about Isak continuing to find the net.

"Yes, with Alex, if he is fit, if he is available, if he is in good shape, I think he will produce the numbers," Iraola told a news conference.

"My demands with Alex will not be about the goals, probably will be about other things. I will demand other things so we can play well, because if we play well we are in good positions and the goals will come.

"He has to contribute towards the collective and knowing when everyone helps, after the goals and assists will come."

Isak stole the headlines on Friday, but both of his strikes were assisted by Cody Gakpo, who could have left Anfield before the transfer deadline, with both Tottenham and Manchester City interested in the Netherlands international.

However, Liverpool blocked a move and Iraola was not surprised by the quality on show from the versatile winger, who produced a fine through-ball for Isak's opener and an even better outside-of-the-foot pass for the second in the ninth minute.

"I had no doubt with Cody. He has been very good all the preseason, has started very well the season, producing numbers," Iraola added.

"After the two assists, he finished as a number nine to help us close the game and I think it's good to have Cody because he can play in the three positions up top. To have him in this place, for the beginning of the season, it's good.

"I think Cody knows how much we value him, I think there is no doubt. I rate him very highly."

France winger Bradley Barcola started on the bench following his £123 million ($166m) transfer from Paris Saint-Germain this week, before being brought on in the 64th minute to make his Liverpool debut.

PA contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Rocchio becomes 6th player with grand slam, walk-off homer in same game, Guardians beat Tigers 7-6
stories.summary: — Brayan Rocchio hit a walk-off homer in the ninth inning after connecting on a tying grand slam in the fourth, rallying the Cleveland Guardians to a 7-6 comeback victory over the Detroit Tigers in the first game of a split doubleheader on Friday.
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- — Brayan Rocchio hit a walk-off homer in the ninth inning after connecting on a tying grand slam in the fourth, rallying the Cleveland Guardians to a 7-6 comeback victory over the Detroit Tigers in the first game of a split doubleheader on Friday.


Rocchio became the sixth player in MLB history with a grand slam and a walk-off in the same game. The last was Boston's Jack Clark on July 31, 1991.


With the win, the Guardians remained in the final American League wild-card position.


Cleveland scored six unanswered runs after falling behind 6-1 in the third, capped by Rocchio's leadoff homer to left field in the ninth off Drew Sommers (1-4). It was his third career walk-off home run and his initial grand slam.


Cade Smith (4-1) pitched the ninth for the win, which was the Guardians’ third in seven games on their critical homestand. The Tigers fell to 4-15 since Aug. 14.


Detroit pushed its lead out to 6-1 in the third on Spencer Torkelson's solo homer off Slade Cecconi before the Guardians erupted for five in the fourth. Travis Bazzana had an RBI single before Rocchio sent Keider Montero’s pitch 366 feet over the fence in right.


Rookies Max Clark and Ben Malgeri each had two-run singles in the first, when the Tigers scored four times against Logan Allen in his first start since July 18. Gleyber Torres had two singles and two runs in the first two innings.


Montero allowed six runs in four innings, while Allen gave up five in 2 1/3 innings. Clark had three singles.


The first pitch was delayed by 1 hour and 4 minutes because of rain.


Up next
Tigers LHP Andrew Sears (0-1, 6.75 ERA) faces Guardians LHP Foster Griffin (15-4, 3.21) in the second game. National League All-Star Griffin is 3-1 in five starts with Cleveland.


------

stories.headline: Sky owner calls Kanter Freedom's free speech lawsuit 'meritless'
stories.summary: Chicago Sky owner Michael Alter called a lawsuit filed by Enes Kanter Freedom "meritless and frivolous" Friday afternoon.
stories.body:
Chicago Sky owner Michael Alter called a lawsuit filed by Enes Kanter Freedom "meritless and frivolous" Friday afternoon.

Kanter Freedom alleged that his First Amendment rights were violated when he was removed from a Sky home game Aug. 23 and then banned from attending Sky games at the arena. The former NBA player was removed from the building after getting in a verbal altercation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter against the Indiana Fever. He was sitting courtside in a black T-shirt that read: "WOMAN noun. adult human female."

Kanter Freedom put up his arms and began to walk toward the court from his baseline seat as he and Cloud exchanged words. He stepped past media camera operators to approach the floor; security stopped him and subsequently ejected him. Alter had previously explained that Kanter Freedom made himself "the potential to be a threat" by stepping toward the court and players.

A 15-page complaint was filed Thursday in the Northern District of Illinois Eastern Division and listed the defendants as the Sky, the city of Chicago, and Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority, which owns and operates Wintrust Arena

"This lawsuit is meritless and frivolous," Alter said in a statement Friday. "Freedom's claim that he was removed from Wintrust Arena due to his speech is false. As his own complaint acknowledges, he wore the shirt in question for multiple hours without any contact with security. Security removed Freedom only after he violated fan code of conduct by rising from his seat, gesturing at a player, and stepping toward the court.

"Freedom was removed for his conduct, not his speech. We look forward to the truth prevailing in court."

Kanter Freedom has inserted himself in the political realm in recent years and has been vocal in the national debate sparked by Fever guard Sophie Cunningham's comments regarding transgender athletes. He and former NBA player Royce White recently declared themselves women and eligible to play in the WNBA. They are not eligible to play in the league, multiple sources told ESPN.

On social media, Kanter Freedom posted that he was "peacefully exercising" his First Amendment rights.

"My T-shirt did what the whole WNBA apparently couldn't: define a woman," Kanter Freedom wrote. "No threats. No violence. Just biology. And somehow, that required a security escort.

"You don't have to agree with my speech but you don't get to silence me for it. I will not be intimidated. I will not be silenced. I will continue to stand for women and defend free speech."

stories.headline: PSG give coach Luis Enrique, 5 players new contracts
stories.summary: Paris Saint-Germain have rewarded coach Luis Enrique and five members of their squad with new contracts after helping the French club to back-to-back Champions League titles.
stories.body:
Paris Saint-Germain have rewarded coach Luis Enrique and five members of their squad with new contracts after helping the French club to back-to-back Champions League titles.

Luis Enrique, 56, who was previously in charge of Barcelona and the Spain national team, joined PSG in July 2023 and has won the Ligue 1 title in each of his three seasons in the French capital.

His biggest achievement, however, has been ending the club's wait to land a first Champions League title. After a dominant 5-0 win over Inter Milan to lift the trophy for the first time in 2025, Luis Enrique repeated the trick last season by leading them past Arsenal in the final of Europe's top competition.

In total, Luis Enrique has won 13 titles with PSG since his arrival. His previous contract was due to expire next summer.

PSG also announced a raft of contract extensions for important members of the squad on Friday, with Lucas Beraldo, Senny Mayulu, João Neves and Willian Pacho signing new deals until 2031.

Spain's World Cup winner Fabián Ruiz has extended his stay until 2028.

PSG have drawn both their opening Ligue 1 matches this season ahead of Friday's visit of AS Monaco. They will begin the defense of their Champions League title against Slovan Bratislava on Wednesday.

PA contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Flavio Briatore takes aim at McLaren and 'nasty' judge after Pierre Gasly ruling
stories.summary: Flavio Briatore has accused a "nasty" FIA judge of having a "working relationship" with McLaren in an extraordinary outburst against the British team on the eve of Sunday's Italian Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Flavio Briatore has accused a "nasty" FIA judge of having a "working relationship" with McLaren in an extraordinary outburst against the British team on the eve of Sunday's Italian Grand Prix.

The controversial Briatore -- who had a lifetime Formula 1 ban overturned for fixing the 2008 Singapore Grand Prix -- arrived for Friday's team representative news conference armed with an A4 piece of paper.

He proceeded to take aim at McLaren, just hours after it had been confirmed that Alpine driver Pierre Gasly had been stripped of his podium from June's Monaco Grand Prix.

Gasly finished third at the round in Monte Carlo only to be hit with two five-second penalties for speeding in the pit lane.

The sanctions dropped him to seventh -- elevating Red Bull's Isack Hadjar to third. Alpine appealed against the post-race punishment and Gasly was reinstated. However, that decision was undone following a protest by McLaren and Red Bull at an FIA International Court of Appeal (ICA) hearing last month. Hadjar reclaimed third and McLaren's Oscar Piastri moved up one place to fourth.

Filippo Marchino was among one of four judges overseeing the case. But Briatore suggested the American-Italian lawyer was in cahoots with McLaren.

He alleged the British team has previously provided an international non-profit organisation, One Drop Foundation, of which Marchino serves as a director, with "two or three McLaren cars."

- Italian Grand Prix: Charles Leclerc leads Lewis Hamilton to a Ferrari one-two in first practice

- F1 to launch 2027 season with Milan festival featuring drivers, all 11 teams

- Italian Grand Prix declared heat hazard; second race this season

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella described Briatore's accusations as "insulting," "disrespectful," and warned he will have to "take responsibility" for his remarks.

"It is very unfair, but we accept the decision," said Alpine chief Briatore. "But what is very strange was the fourth judge in the panel. One of the judges acted like a prosecutor.

"This is not a big problem. The problem is that it is very linked with the McLaren company. We have a nice picture of this guy [Marchino] at a speech for McLaren in 2018 in Beverly Hills.

"He made a foundation. It's called One Drop Foundation. And McLaren gave two or three McLaren cars. So, what is unfair is that some judge was linked with one of the teams that is fighting us.

"The judge normally needs to be independent completely. Filippo Marchino is a judge and he was very nasty during the hearing. And afterwards we found out why this guy was so nasty, he is linked with McLaren.

"The judge has to be independent and not somebody doing a speech for McLaren, and somebody using the McLaren car in the charity. To find out the judge had a very good relationship -- a working relationship -- with McLaren was very disappointing."

In response, Stella, sitting to Briatore's left, fired back: "I find that this conference going in this direction is quite insulting for McLaren, for the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect.

"And if anybody makes these kinds of allegations -- which seem quite serious -- they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum.

"The hearing, the whole International Court of Appeal, was conducted to the highest standards, and we should not question this space like it's been done."

An FIA spokesperson said: "The eligibility of candidates for membership of the International Tribunal and International Court of Appeal is checked by the eligibility assessment committee (EAC), in accordance with the FIA statutes.

"The FIA judicial and disciplinary rules (JDR) provide that for each case before the ICA, a judging panel is constituted comprising at least three judges. The members of the judging panel are appointed by the president of the ICA. Candidates who meet the eligibility criteria set forth in the FIA statutes and who are deemed eligible by the EAC are then put forward for election by the FIA general assembly (GA)."

stories.headline: Ben Simmons returning to NBA on 1-year, $3.5M deal with Kings
stories.summary: Ben Simmons is back in the NBA after reaching one-year, $3.5 million deal with the Kings, his agents Max Wiepking, Sean Tribe and Ryan Arney told Andscape and ESPN.
stories.body:
Three-time All-Star Ben Simmons is back in the NBA after agreeing to a one-year, $3.5 million contract with the Sacramento Kings on Friday, his agents Max Wiepking, Sean Tribe and Ryan Arney told Andscape and ESPN's Shams Charania.

Simmons returns to the NBA after missing the 2025-26 season to rehabilitate lingering back and leg injuries. Now healthy, the 6-foot-10, 240-pounder impressed Kings general manager Scott Perry when he worked out for him in Miami and had an hourlong meeting in late August.

Simmons also traveled to Sacramento to visit the Kings and impressed coach Doug Christie and other members of the basketball staff at the team's practice facility Monday where he underwent an in-depth medical exam and conducted an on-court workout.

In the following days, the Kings offered Simmons a contract with the expectation of him being a backup point guard for rookie Darius Acuff Jr. and play positions 1 through 5. For the Kings, Simmons serves as a high-upside reclamation project who still has years left in his perspective prime.

Simmons' stock rose after he played well while being a full participant in a minicamp with the Australia men's basketball national team in early August. The Minnesota Timberwolves and Golden State Warriors expressed interest in Simmons that could have led to a potential training camp invite. The Kings, however, were the only NBA team to offer him contract. A source said Simmons is excited about playing for the Kings and believes the organization will give him the support and opportunity he has hoped for in his return to the NBA.

The Kings finished 22-60 last season, tying for the worst record in the Western Conference. They waived DeMar DeRozan in July and didn't bring back free agent Russell Westbrook, leaving them with a hole at the guard position.

Simmons was the first overall pick by the Philadelphia 76ers in the 2016 NBA draft out of LSU. The Melbourne, Australia, native won the 2018 NBA Rookie of the Year award and was an NBA All-Defensive first-team selection in 2020.

The 30-year-old's NBA career has also included numerous challenges, including missing the 2016-17 season with a foot injury and missing the 2021-22 season amid a trade holdout, mental health concerns and various physical ailments.

Simmons has averaged 13.1 points, 7.4 rebounds, 7.2 assists and 1.5 steals in 383 regular-season games for the 76ers, Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers. After being waived in February 2025 following a buyout with the Nets, Simmons averaged 2.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 3.1 assists in 18 games for the Clippers while playing limited minutes and fighting back issues. Simmons' last NBA game was Game 5 of the first round against the Denver Nuggets.

He told Andscape in July that he felt as healthy as he had in years and believed he was ready to return to the NBA.

During his NBA hiatus, he purchased a 50% ownership stake in the South Florida Sails professional angling club in December 2025, becoming the team's controlling operator.

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey forward tiers: Who to draft and when to take them
stories.summary: Use these forward tiers to help you plan out your fantasy hockey draft strategy.
stories.body:
Picture the boarding line at the airport.

They call Group 1, and here's the thing about Group 1, it does not matter one bit where in that group you're standing. First person or last, you're strolling on with your bag and your pick of the overhead bin. Everyone in the group is, functionally, the same.

Then they call Group 2 ... still totally fine, still getting your bag up top. Group 3, you're eyeing the bins nervously, but at least you're all in the same boat. Er, plane.

By the time they're calling Group 6, you're handing your carry-on to the gate agent and hoping to see it in the next time zone -- but so is everyone else in your group.

That drop, from group to group, real and steep, with near-total equality inside each group? That's a tier list. That's the whole idea. And that's how you should draft.

Here's why it saves you at a draft. Say you've got your eye on one guy, and the two picks ahead of you snap him and the player right next to him up. On a flat ranking, you panic. Scramble down to whatever's left with the clock screaming at you. But if you already knew those two were sitting in the same boarding group as three other players you rated just as highly? You don't flinch. You wave the next one aboard and you've lost nothing.

That's the magic -- you stop making 150 individual decisions and start making a handful of "anyone in this group is fine" ones. It's the same reason you don't need to stampede toward the jetway when your group is called. Everyone in it lands in the same place.

The fantasy forward groups below are mine. My projections, my drop-offs, my problem when I'm wrong. They aren't the official in-game ranks you'll see inside the ESPN Fantasy Hockey.

These come from my own projections: a base of each player's three-year average, a sprinkle of how comparable players the same age have fared across the past 15 seasons, and a dash of manual adjustment for the spots where my gut overrules the math. The projected ESPN standard points sit right next to each name below, so you can see exactly where I've got everyone slotted.

Note: Points based on the ESPN standard scoring system.

stories.headline: Tata Martino warns Atlanta vs. Miami: No way to neutralize Messi
stories.summary: Atlanta United FC head coach Gerardo "Tata" Martino warned his players of Lionel Messi's capabilities on the field ahead of the MLS regular season clash against Inter Miami CF on Saturday at Nu Stadium.
stories.body:
Atlanta United head coach Gerardo "Tata" Martino warned his players of Lionel Messi's capabilities on the field ahead of the MLS regular season clash against Inter Miami on Saturday at Nu Stadium.

"We've just seen what he did at the World Cup at the age of 39, everything that happened in a match went through him. There's no team capable of neutralizing him for the entire 92 or 93 or 95 minutes of the match," Martino said.

"There is always a decisive moment. Sometimes there are many moments in a match, at other times, like in the game against England, it comes down to a single moment, and then it's over. There is no turning back. I told the players: even if we control the match for 89 minutes, we could still lose it."

Martino will face the Herons for the first time since resigning as Inter Miami manager in November 2024. He announced his shocking departure from the club days after being eliminated from the 2024 MLS Cup playoffs, citing "personal reasons."

Martino joined Inter Miami in June 2023 before leading the club to its first two titles in history with the 2023 Leagues Cup trophy and 2024 Supporters' Shield. He also inspired Miami to break the league record for most points in a single season.

Martino returned to MLS in November 2025 to lead Atlanta United for a second time.

He previously led Atlanta United from 2016 to 2018, serving as the club's first ever head coach. Martino also propelled Atlanta to the 2018 MLS Cup title before departing to join the Mexico national team.

Atlanta United currently sits in 13th place on the Eastern Conference table with 21 points in 22 games after a rocky start to the season.

stories.headline: What we learned: The Cats are kings of the grind; no shame in Carlton's end
stories.summary: The Cats ended Carlton's fairytale run to September with a grinding effort that should have the Dockers worried. As for the Blues? There was no shame in their 2026 curtain call. Here's what we learned from the game.
stories.body:
Geelong ended Carlton's 2026 AFL season on Friday night, winning by 33 points in front of a mammoth elimination final crowd of 96,680 at the MCG.

Patrick Dangerfield wound back the clock kicking five majors, and Shaun Mannagh starred as the Cats set up a date with Fremantle next Friday night in a win-or-go-home semifinal.

Here are three things we learned from the game:

No one grinds down an opponent like Geelong
Carlton knew it had to start well. It was the underdog. Up against one of the most finals-hardened outfits football has seen. And had already survived a cut-throat encounter while its opponent put its feet up.

The Blues couldn't have made a better fist of that opening, either. Four goals to one in the first term, and by the time Ollie Hollands converted midway through the second, Carlton was 21 points up.

And in the end, it still counted for little. Because no one grinds down an opponent like Geelong. And in perfect conditions for the grind -- wet, slippery, with strong bodies required at the contest -- the Cats were in their element.

First Geelong got the game back on its terms with some basics. It tightened up defensively, and it applied more physical pressure. The tackle count said it all, Carlton ahead 19-7 at the first change, the Cats laying 25 to 13 in the second term.

The Cats started winning the contest, they pressed harder up on Carlton's defence, forcing more turnovers. And sure enough, the scoreboard became another trend to follow suit.

Harry McKay gave Carlton a seven-point lead nine minutes into the second half. But the Blues' next goal wouldn't arrive until Geelong had kicked eight in a row to lead by 42 points and completely blow to shreds what had looked set to be a tight game.

Patrick Dangerfield rightfully gets the plaudits for a superb five-goal, 21-disposal performance, Tom Stewart was masterful as ever in defence, Bailey Smith prolific through the middle.

But the Cats have been less star-driven for a while now, and two players just as pivotal to this victory were Shaun Mannagh and Ollie Wiltshire.

It was Mannagh who was the key to turning the midfield tide when Carlton threatened to build a gap too difficult for the Cats to bridge. And it was Wiltshire who engineered the goals which did just that, two goals assists in a row in the second term the start of Geelong's fightback.

The clever small forward ended up with four goal assists and could have kicked several himself. And there were probably still plenty of Carlton fans by the end of his contribution wondering who No. 21 for their opponent was.

That's the Cats, though. Efficient. No fuss. And at their best with something on the line. Like finals.

Still wondering about the wildcard?
Last week, the debate was hard to contest. Two blockbuster MCG finals, crowds of 173,000 and one epic finish. Did Friday night offer an argument for the negative?

Perhaps in a contest sense. This was 5th versus 10th remember, and for most of the second half it looked like it, an eventual 33-point margin perhaps flattering Carlton, the Cats posting 37 scores to just 19.

Then again, Carlton did beat the Cats during the season proper. And had we retained the top eight this season, Friday night at the G would have seen Geelong up against the Western Bulldogs, whom the Cats disposed of by an effortless 75 points back in Round 6.

And yes, if you're talking revenue, and let's be honest, that's all this has ever been about, the advocates have a pretty decent argument in the crowd at this game, a massive 96,680, the second-largest ever for an elimination final and meaning that 10th-placed team has pulled 188,000 people through the turnstiles in two weeks.

This writer remains a wildcard sceptic, but is happy to concede those sort of numbers are going to be hard to dismiss.

No shame in Carlton's curtain call
That huge crowd had just about halved by the finish of Geelong's big win, so dominant were the Cats in the early stages of the last quarter until Carlton got a few "cheapies".

But really, nothing could detract from where the Blues have finished this season compared with the train wreck it looked like before the midway point.

A team which looked destined for the bottom four instead contested September and a list which looked at best pedestrian in the end had excitement bobbing up all over the place, Jagga Smith, Harry Dean, Talor Byrne, and Billy Wilson just a sample of what Blues fans have to look forward to in 2027.

No wonder coach Josh Fraser was taking the positive route at the post-match press conference despite the decisive nature of his team's loss.

"There is work ahead of us and we won't settle on mediocrity," he said. "We need to chase that success and there is an expectation on the way their break looks and the way they return.

"There is a lot of work we have to do. Some of it is marginal, some of it is bigger, but we can't turn up in pre-season and think this will just roll on. We have to continue to look at our game and get better. I don't want to be sitting here finishing in eighth position.

"That's some challenges we have to embrace, and there is no evidence they won't do that as they've done an outstanding job over the last 15 weeks."

They certainly have. Ask any Carlton fan what they expected to be doing in the first week of September when the Blues were 1-8 and 16th on the ladder after Round 9 and you can bet your life the answer wouldn't have been: "Watching my team play in a final."

They may get to watch a few more over the next few seasons, too.

stories.headline: Arrow takes centre stage: Life and sport inseparably, intrinsically linked
stories.summary: Jai Arrow has handled this awful situation as well as a person possibly can, and deserves everything and anything we can give him.
stories.body:
Remember that old Bill Shankly quote about football being far more than a matter of life and death? It's fun to say, it reminds us of just how much these games mean, and why we waste hours and hours of our weeks watching, reading about or thinking about them.

It is, of course, also partly tongue-in-cheek. And on a night like this you could be forgiven for dismissing such an idea as complete nonsense. You see Jai Arrow, his condition deteriorating, everything being slowly taken from him, and it does make you wonder what the point of any of this is, if something so awful can happen to someone for no reason.

But the lesson is that it's not that this stuff, which is for all intents and purposes a leisure activity, is more or less important. It's that sports and life and death aren't things that we need to think about as being independent of one another. They're inseparably, intrinsically linked.

Death and pain and suffering and loss are horrible experiences, but it's the things that cause us grief that allow us to truly embrace the things that make us great. And ignoring everything else about Motor Neurone Disease and ignoring the pocket of snarky people who had a problem with Arrow playing these final two matches, this was truly great. A port in a storm of what will continue to be a long and hard road for a champion player, as well as his friends and family.

Thankfully, we left the banality of people being upset about Arrow's chance to reach 100 games in the discourse leading up to game 99, when the scenes of Arrow being unable to even dress himself or put his boots on were probably enough to make those people realise that the sanctity of the sport, whatever that means, really didn't matter all that much when juxtaposed with what was happening in front of them, and what we saw again last night.

This isn't anyone wheeling out a sick man for performative reasons. This isn't a horrible disease being used as a prop for altruism. Anyone who was there last week on the Gold Coast or last night in Sydney can see how much all of this meant to him. Arrow has done brilliantly to make the best of this situation at every turn, including a mocking dismissal of substitute Cam Murray at the start of last week's win over the Titans. He's handled this awful situation as well as a person possibly can, and deserves everything and anything we can give him.

It's funny how things work out. For all the talk of wild card rounds, mass restings, games having no stakes in the final round of the season and potential remedies to these issues, it ended up being for the best, as something more important than any two competition points took centre stage.

If Souths had lost last week and the Sharks had won, the Roosters would be full-strength and the Rabbitohs would need to beat their arch-rivals to make the finals - the reverse of what happened in the final round last year. In a way, the low stakes of this match and the team the Roosters put on the field meant that this really was all about Jai Arrow.

Arrow, of course, would not have wanted his own story to distract from a potential play-in game for Souths, even if nobody but the very worst of our society would have seen it that way. But instead, much like the Alex Johnston game earlier this year, the atmosphere was about as far from 'Book of Feuds' as you could get. The crowd rose as one when bench player Cody Walker came to the sideline, and special interchange official Wayne Bennett stood with card in hand. Each man embraced Arrow, who received the loudest cheer of the night, and perhaps any night at that stadium.

The game itself meandered on. Souths scored 50 points without looking particularly good, the young Roosters looked game despite losing by 30. None of that mattered.

On Friday, Arrow was the storyline. He was more important than the result - and would have been even if it was a grand final. But he IS sports, and the way that people around not just the NRL but the Australian and even international sporting communities have rallied around him, is life.

stories.headline: Brayan Rocchio's walk-off homer gives Guardians a 7-6 comeback win over Tigers
stories.summary: — Brayan Rocchio hit a walk-off homer in the ninth inning after connecting on a tying grand slam in the fourth, rallying the Cleveland Guardians to a 7-6 comeback victory over the Detroit Tigers in the first game of a split doubleheader on Friday.
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- — Brayan Rocchio hit a walk-off homer in the ninth inning after connecting on a tying grand slam in the fourth, rallying the Cleveland Guardians to a 7-6 comeback victory over the Detroit Tigers in the first game of a split doubleheader on Friday.


With the win, the Guardians remained in the final American League wild-card position.


Rocchio led off the ninth with a homer to left field off Drew Sommers (1-4), giving Cleveland six unanswered runs to end the contest after falling behind 6-1 in the third. His third career walk-off home run followed his first grand slam.


Cade Smith (4-1) pitched the ninth for the win, which was the Guardians’ third in seven games on their critical homestand. The Tigers fell to 4-15 since Aug. 14.


Detroit pushed its lead out to 6-1 in the third on Spencer Torkelson's solo homer off Slade Cecconi before the Guardians erupted for five in the fourth. Travis Bazzana had an RBI single before Rocchio sent Keider Montero’s pitch 366 feet over the fence in right.


Rookies Max Clark and Ben Malgeri each had two-run singles in the first, when the Tigers scored four times against Logan Allen in his first start since July 18. Gleyber Torres had two singles and two runs in the first two innings.


Montero allowed six runs in four innings, while Allen gave up five in 2 1/3 innings. Clark had three singles.


The first pitch was delayed by 1 hour and 4 minutes because of rain.

Tigers LHP Andrew Sears (0-1, 6.75 ERA) faces Guardians LHP Foster Griffin (15-4, 3.21) in the second game. National League All-Star Griffin is 3-1 in five starts with Cleveland.

stories.headline: What WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert's retirement means
stories.summary: What does the league need from its next commissioner after Cathy Engelbert retires? Is the WNBA better off now than when she took over?
stories.byline: Michael Voepel and Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland
stories.body:
The WNBA has changed substantially since Cathy Engelbert -- who announced Friday she will retire at the end of this year -- took over in 2019. Her tenure included two collective bargaining agreements, an enormous increase in franchise valuations, expansion that will reach 18 teams by 2030 and a much greater global footprint.

Engelbert gets a lot of credit for that, but she also received plenty of criticism in her seven years, especially regarding her relationships with players.

What legacy does Engelbert leave behind? What traits should the WNBA be looking for in its next commissioner? And what will that leader's priorities be in their first year? ESPN examines the WNBA commissioner's job: the person who is leaving it and what awaits the person who takes over.

What is Engelbert's legacy as WNBA commissioner?

Michael Voepel: I've covered the WNBA since Day 1 and have worked with every WNBA leader. (They were called presidents until the title was changed for Engelbert's tenure.) Each brought her own skill set and led the league at different stages of growth. Val Ackerman was a lawyer who was instrumental in launching the league. Donna Orender worked at boosting visibility while also keeping the league alive during the global financial crisis of 2007-09. Laurel J. Richie was the first Black woman to take the league's leadership role, and Lisa Borders, also a Black woman with an extensive business background, navigated the more public actions players began to take with social justice initiatives.

Engelbert, previously CEO at Deloitte, came from the financial world, and at her first news conference in 2019 she stated her goals as expanding the league, making it financially viable and improving the player experience. All of those things have happened. Whatever Engelbert's missteps, the league is in a far better place as she leaves it.

Kendra Andrews: Though Engelbert had many wins during her tenure, I think the past year marked with tension with her players will overshadow everything else. When Napheesa Collier sat at the podium during her exit interview in September 2025 and shared the most public criticism an athlete has voiced about a commissioner, and then had her peers back her up, that became Engelbert's legacy. Since then, there has hardly been any positive review of Engelbert from WNBA players.

People will remember the boos that rained down on her at the Commissioner's Cup finals and WNBA All-Star Weekends. They will remember how long and contentious the 2026 CBA negotiations were, and they will remember how multiple figures around the league called for a new leader.

Two things can be true: Engelbert drove a lot of success in the league, and she was not beloved by players. The latter is what she will be remembered for.

Kareem Copeland: Time will likely forget the dustups -- the rocky relationship with players, slow-playing advancements in travel and other leaguewide accommodations, a tendency to be overconcerned about the older ownership groups while the league was growing with owners willing to invest more heavily. The bottom line is the league will have expanded to its highest number of teams in league history when Detroit and Cleveland arrive, expanded to the most games in league history, signed the biggest media deal in women's sports history and landed a CBA that transformed the league into a new era with the first million-dollar salaries. When people look back in 10-20 years, that's what will be remembered.

What were Engelbert's biggest wins as WNBA commissioner?

Andrews: Executing the WNBA bubble during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 was a huge accomplishment for Engelbert. The 22-game season played in Florida against the backdrop of a deadly pandemic and national upheaval following the deaths of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor shined a new spotlight on the WNBA. It allowed the league to dedicate that season to social injustices, but also the viewership and level of play produced in the Wubble set the league up for a level of success over the next five years no one could have expected, especially given the circumstances. That condensed 2020 season, which occurred on the heels of the 2020 CBA agreement, set the W up for growth and exposure that has helped get the league to where it is today.

Copeland: The 2026 CBA is the easy answer, and navigating the environment around COVID and the racial injustices of 2020 were massive wins. But the simple act of moving to chartered flights, despite Engelbert's hesitation to do so for years, was so much more than a convenience move. That affected player health, how the league could schedule games, player safety and just the overall cadence of how teams operate throughout the season. Watching entire teams standing next to the traveling public at baggage claim was a sight to see. The one simple act touched on so many areas throughout the league that it's funny to think that it was just in 2022 that the New York Liberty were fined $500,000 for chartering flights.

Voepel: From a purely financial aspect, the fact that franchise valuations skyrocketed during Engelbert's tenure has been her biggest win. That's what led to improved travel, facilities and expansion. When James Dolan put the New York Liberty on the market in November 2017, he essentially said the team was of no value to him. Joe and Clara Wu Tsai bought the franchise in early 2019 for between $10-15 million. Now the Liberty have been valued as high as $600 million. The popularity of the individual players like Caitlin Clark and the league as a whole have greatly increased what the franchises are worth. But those increases happened with Engelbert at the helm.

In what areas did Engelbert struggle as commissioner?

Andrews: One piece of feedback from a player is that Engelbert was too reactionary. Rarely was she -- or the league -- ahead of the problems facing the WNBA and its players; player safety and online hate and abuse are examples. When it comes to the Internet, there is only so much that can be done. But the complaint was rooted in how much the issue escalated before the league publicly addressed it.

Some also found Engelbert's reaction to those issues to be lackluster. In September 2024, Engelbert failed to condemn racist and vitriolic behavior surrounding the Caitlin Clark-Angel Reese rivalry, instead telling CNBC that rivalries are good for the league. She later said she "missed the mark" with her initial statement and said it was a learning moment for her. She followed that by saying there is "no room for racism, misogyny [and] homophobia in the WNBA," but it was another missed opportunity to swiftly shut down a topic that has since grown into a major issue in WNBA discourse.

Voepel: To Kendra's points, Engelbert misjudged how to respond to players' concerns and wasn't able to build enough allies among either the owners or the players.

Some detractors also might point to the 2022 capital raise, when the WNBA sold a 16% equity stake to investors for $75 million, as a big mistake by Engelbert. But that move has to be taken in the context of when it happened: The WNBA badly needed that cash infusion, and the league's rapid growth since then was hardly expected. In early 2022, the "Caitlin Clark Effect" had yet to fully blossom -- it took off in 2023, her junior year at Iowa -- and the WNBA was still recovering from the 2020 pandemic season. So I don't see that capital raise as a failure so much as unfortunate timing, taking the circumstances into account.

Who might be in the discussions to take the job next?

Voepel: Bethany Donaphin, head of league operations, knows well what the commissioner's job entails and briefly played in the WNBA after her college career at Stanford.

Two other names some have suggested are former player Swin Cash and soon-to-retire Los Angeles Sparks forward Nneka Ogwumike, the longtime president of the players association. Cash has management experience from her time as a senior vice president with the NBA's New Orleans Pelicans. Ogwumike has plenty of experience with the league thanks to her involvement in two past CBAs, but she has been on the opposite side of the table. As commissioner, she would need to work for the owners.

Ultimately, this is a huge hire for Silver, who will be appointing the head of the WNBA for the third time since he became NBA commissioner in 2014.

What does the WNBA need from Engelbert's successor, especially in the first year?
Voepel: First off, repairing the relationship between both current and former players and the commissioner's office. That wasn't Engelbert's strength, and it damaged the perception of her tenure. The new commissioner must establish trust with the players. But the players must bear their share of responsibility in this, too. It has been easy for them to put the commissioner or the league on blast for everything they don't like or anything that went wrong in the past few years, even when that hasn't been constructive.

It would seem likely that any new commissioner will have a "honeymoon" period in which many players might be happy just to have someone different. But for the relationship to grow from that, both parties need to communicate and have respect for each other.

What skills or attributes does the next commissioner need?

Voepel: The WNBA commissioner needs to be an accomplished diplomat. There are so many constituencies involved in running a league: Obviously, there are the players. There are owners -- and remember, the commissioner works for them -- many of whom have been with the league for many years and others who are still learning the ropes. There are the fans -- some of whom have followed the league for decades; some who haven't. There are businesses and sponsors who have been with the WNBA a long time but still need to feel appreciated, and those that are new and must be cultivated. And there's the fact that the WNBA commissioner has a boss: the NBA commissioner.

The new commissioner will have to deal with an ever-growing media contingent and fanbase -- some of whom have followed the league for decades and some who haven't.

Engelbert's successor has to find a better way to navigate the racial tensions that everyone knows exist but are challenging to talk about in a constructive way. There are social issues that always seem to get magnified in women's sports.

The WNBA today is barely comparable to seven years ago, in a very good way. But with a bigger ecosystem -- to use one of Engelbert's favorite terms -- comes more opportunities and challenges. Other women's sports are growing, too, and while there is camaraderie there, the WNBA also wants to be the premiere women's sports league in the world. That means grassroots involvement and investment globally in girls' basketball. It means figuring out the WNBA's long-term relationship with Unrivaled. It means being a lot smarter about how to use social media for growth and healthy messaging. The WNBA found some new gears in Engelbert's tenure. Now it's time to really step on the gas.

Copeland: A more congenial relationship with the players is always nice in theory, but the general public often forgets that commissioners work for and represent the owners. There will always be conflict. As Kendra noted above, the league often gets itself in trouble for being slow to react when issues arise as opposed to getting out in front of things. Engelbert had a business background and that was her strong suit, but the league was often reactionary to issues that could be predicted. From problems with officiating to the sale of the Connecticut Sun to player safety and the current transgender conversation, the league was often playing catch-up, which further alienated players.

Is the WNBA better off now than it was when Engelbert took over?

Andrews: Without a doubt, yes. The 2026 WNBA has grown and changed exponentially from the version of the league Engelbert inherited in 2019. Purely from a size standpoint, the WNBA has grown from 12 staff members to nearly 100. The new media rights deal increased the league's economic growth, and the footprint has expanded from 12 teams to 15 (and 18 teams by 2030). Two major CBA deals were negotiated and agreed upon by Engelbert, ensuring the players more pay and benefits (which go to retired players as well), and helping land the first million-dollar contracts in league history. The health and sustainability of the WNBA is in a far better place than it was six years ago, and should be set up for far more success under the next commissioner.

Copeland: The league is in a completely different place today than it was in 2018. Now, Engelbert shouldn't get credit for all the advances, but she certainly played a significant role. Kendra hit all the touchpoints, but one thing that has advanced is the talent level in and entering the league. As the WNBA has grown into a sustainable major professional league in the United States in which players can stay at home and make generational wealth, young girls can have this as a goal in a more advanced way than ever before. The trickle down has been more youth programs and training opportunities for girls than in preceding years. Young girls are taking advantage, growing skills and defining goals earlier. It's not a surprise that there has been an influx of talent coming out of the drafts that are making an immediate and historical impact on the league -- Clark, Paige Bueckers, Reese, Olivia Miles, Sonia Citron and Kiki Iriafen to name a few. The depth and talent level in recent drafts has been more consistent and dependable in recent years. That's not directly related to the commissioner's role, but the growth and advanced state of the WNBA has had a direct impact on the youth ranks, which pays off for the league years later.

stories.headline: George Russell fastest in second practice at Italian Grand Prix, Charles Leclerc behind
stories.summary: George Russell landed a timely world championship boost by finishing fastest in practice for the Italian Grand Prix.
stories.body:
George Russell landed a timely world championship boost by finishing fastest in practice for the Italian Grand Prix.

Russell has won just two of the 12 rounds so far, and he heads into Sunday's race at Monza 59 points behind Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli.

However, Antonelli will serve a grid penalty for exceeding engine parts and is due to start his home event from the back of the field.

Antonelli's sanction provides Russell with a golden opportunity to eat into his teammate's lead, and the Englishman will be able to draw confidence from his speed in practice.

Russell finished 0.120 seconds clear of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc -- who had earlier set the pace in first practice -- with Antonelli 0.141 seconds off the pace.

Lando Norris arrives at the 'Temple of Speed' as a driver in form having won the previous rounds, in Hungary, prior to the summer break, and in the Netherlands a fortnight ago.

However, the world champion, 83 points behind Antonelli did not trouble the top of the order on Friday. Norris finished almost four-tenths behind Russell and a place clear of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

Norris also accused Lance Stroll of "dangerous driving" after he had to take evasive action at the opening chicane to avoid a collision with the Aston Martin driver.

- Alpine's Pierre Gasly stripped of Monaco GP podium after McLaren and Red Bull win appeal

- F1 to launch 2027 season with Milan festival featuring drivers, all 11 teams

- Flavio Briatore takes aim at McLaren and 'nasty' judge after Pierre Gasly ruling

Seven-time world champion Hamilton is armed here with an engine upgrade and spoke on Thursday about the "phenomenal" prospect of taking a record sixth win at the 'Temple of Speed,' and a first as a Ferrari driver.

Hamilton finished second to teammate Leclerc in the opening running, but was then half-a-second back later in the day, to deal a provisional dent in his victory bid, and his aspirations of a record eighth title. Like Russell, he is 59 points behind Antonelli in the standings.

Hamilton was one of five Brits in the top eight, with Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad seventh and Haas driver Oliver Bearman a place behind.

Max Verstappen struggled with the handling of his Red Bull, and could manage only ninth on an underwhelming afternoon for the four-time world champion.

stories.headline: 2026 NBA buzz: Latest free agency and trade updates
stories.summary: We're tracking deals, trades and buzz across the NBA, including the latest on Kawhi Leonard and the NBA's investigation into the Clippers.
stories.body:
NBA free agency has almost reached the end, with several players landing in new homes this offseason.

LeBron James decided to continue his historic career with the Philadelphia 76ers after months of deliberation. The Sixers also traded for Jaylen Brown this summer, turning the franchise into a true contender with two huge moves.

Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo is headed to South Beach to team up with Bam Adebayo and the Miami Heat, and the Los Angeles Lakers have been sold for the second time in 10 months.

What will happen next during this turbulent offseason?

Check back here for all the latest buzz, news and reactions from our ESPN NBA insiders, with the latest info at the top:

Quick links:

Free agency grades | Trade grades

Trade tracker | Transactions

Depth charts | Trade machine | More

Sept. 4

Ben Simmons signs with Kings on one-year deal

Three-time All-Star Ben Simmons has agreed to a one-year, $3.5 million deal with the Sacramento Kings, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. The deal marks a return to the NBA for Simmons, who sat out the 2025-26 season. Simmons was the No. 1 pick in the 2016 NBA draft.

Sept. 3

Windhorst: Steve Ballmer 'very' angry after NBA penalty
ESPN's Brian Windhorst reported that LA Clippers owner Steve Ballmer is 'very angry' after the penalties handed down to the franchise by the NBA on Sept. 2.

"When you're worth $150 billion and you're angry, and he's very clearly angry, you can't advise him, you can't talk to him," Windhorst said on Get Up. "I'd be stunned if his lawyers didn't advise him, as Shams [Charania] said, to make a plea deal because he should've made a please deal."

Read more: NBA punishes Clippers after Kawhi investigation: Top questions​

Thompson, Rockets agree to five-year contract extension

The Houston Rockets and Amen Thompson have agreed to a five-year, $208 million rookie-scale contract extension, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania The deal includes a 10% trade kicker.

Sept. 2

NBA insiders answer the biggest questions on NBA's Clippers investigation
After the NBA released the findings of its yearlong investigation into allegations that the LA Clippers circumvented the salary cap in order to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard, ESPN NBA insiders Baxter Holmes, Brian Windhorst, Ramona Shelburne and Bobby Marks examined the report, the massive punishments the NBA leveled and how all of it could impact this season -- and beyond.

The punishment was compounded by the Clippers being previous offenders during Steve Ballmer's tenure as owner. They were fined $250,000 for a similar accusation involving DeAndre Jordan in 2015. There also was a 2019 investigation into Leonard's signing in which the Clippers were cleared of wrongdoing but subsequently warned and put through a seminar to remind them of the rules.
This penalty is indeed harsh, but it could have been worse.

In the case of Joe Smith and the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2000, his contract was voided and his Bird rights were vacated.

Leonard will have to write a sizable check -- $700,000 -- but he will not be suspended, and his contract and Bird rights remain unaffected.

The Clippers and the Toronto Raptors will be allowed to move forward in their trade process, one league source said. If the trade moves forward, LA will acquire two first-round picks in the deal. -- Windhorst

Read the full story here.

Charania: NBA rules on Kawhi Leonard-Aspiration investigation

Sources told ESPN's Shams Charania reported that, after a year-long probe into Kawhi Leonard-Aspiration connection, the NBA has stripped the LA Clippers of five first-round picks and issued a $30 million fine to owner Steve Ballmer, as well as suspended Ballmer, Lawrence Frank and Gillian Zucker.

On top of that, Leonard will have to pay $700,000 in restitution for improper benefits by the franchise for his uncle and former business representative, Dennis Robertson. Leonard will not be suspended but Robertson is banned by the NBA from all business dealings.

SEC requesting information from Daktronics regarding Clippers probe
The Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking information from Daktronics, the company that designed the LA Clippers' videoboard inside the Intuit Dome, related to Kawhi Leonard, a company executive said Wednesday.

"Let me now briefly address a matter that has been in the media concerning the NBA's investigation of Kawhi Leonard and the Clippers in connection with the league's collective bargaining agreement that many of you may have heard about," chief financial officer Howard Atkins said on Daktronics' quarterly earnings call.

"As you might expect, we have received requests for information from the NBA. Additionally, the Securities and Exchange Commission is seeking information from us concerning the company and Mr. Leonard. "We take these requests seriously and are cooperating. At this point, out of respect for the respective processes, we will not be providing further comment."

A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment.

Podcaster Pablo Torre reported last month that Daktronics had an undisclosed sponsorship agreement allegedly worth millions of dollars with Leonard.

Torre interviewed someone identified as an "anonymous high-level source under contract for Intuit Dome" who alleged that the sponsorship deal "was 1,000% a way to circumvent the salary cap. It was funneling money from the Clippers through Daktronics back to Kawhi."

The NBA launched its investigation into the Clippers and Leonard last September after numerous podcasts from Torre, who cited internal documents that showed that Clippers owner Steve Ballmer invested $50 million in Aspiration, a now-defunct green banking company, through his personal LLC in September 2021.

That month, the Clippers signed a 23-year, $300 million deal with Aspiration, making the company the "first founding partner" of the Intuit Dome.

Six months later, Aspiration signed its $28 million endorsement deal with Leonard.

An unnamed employee who purportedly worked for the banking company told Torre that Leonard's sponsorship deal "was to circumvent the salary cap."

The Clippers have repeatedly denied that they funneled money through Aspiration to compensate Leonard.

On Aug. 17, ESPN reported that the NBA has found no evidence showing Ballmer funneled money through team sponsors to pay Leonard in order to circumvent the salary cap, per three people with knowledge of recent discussions between the two sides. -- Baxter Holmes

Sept. 1

Windhorst: Sabonis hired new agent this summer, could want out of Sacramento

On the Sept. 1 episode of "The Hoop Collective," ESPN's Brian Windhorst discussed what Domantas Sabonis hiring a new agent this summer could mean for his future with the Sacramento Kings.

Windhorst on Sabonis hiring a new agent: " I do think it's somewhat interesting that he changed agents this offseason. He hired Aaron Mintz of CAA. Steve Heumann and that group. One of the top executives at CAA. This last year, Mintz and his group executed the trade for Trae Young away from Atlanta, executed the trade for Walker Kessler away from the [Jazz]. Domantas Sabonis just hired him.

"At the risk of ... parodying myself from the season, why would he do that?"

Aug. 29

Latest on Curry's next deal decision

The window for Stephen Curry to sign an extension has officially opened.

The four-time champion and two-time MVP is now eligible (through June 30) to sign a two-year, $136.7 million extension. If he signs, Curry will become the first player in NBA history to rack up more than $600 million in on-court earnings.

A new contract for Curry will have important financial implications for Golden State. With Curry, Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III able to become free agents after the 2026-27 season, Golden State could have significant cap space to reshape its roster.

If Curry signs for the maximum allowed in the first season of an extension ($65.7 million), the Warriors project to have between $45 million and $60 million in cap space next offseason. -- Bobby Marks

Wolves, Jazz swap forwards
The Minnesota Timberwolves are trading forward Josh Green to the Utah Jazz for forwards Cody Williams and John Konchar, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

The Wolves are expected to keep Williams, the No. 10 pick in 2024, and waive-and-stretch Konchar, sources said. By moving Green's $14.7 million salary, Minnesota can sign Jonathan Kuminga to the taxpayer midlevel exception.

Aug. 27

Free agent center Richards agrees to one-year deal with Heat
Free agent center Nick Richards has agreed to a one-year deal with the Miami Heat, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. After signing Klay Thompson, the Heat fill roster slot No. 14 with a reserve big man.

Aug. 26

Kuminga signs two-year deal with Minnesota
Free agent forward Jonathan Kuminga agreed to a two-year, $12.4 million deal with the Minnesota Timberwolves, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Kuminga probably will start alongside Anthony Edwards, LaMelo Ball, Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert.

Mathurin to sign with Pels
Free agent guard Bennedict Mathurin agreed to a two-year, $16 million deal with the New Orleans Pelicans, including a player option, sources tell ESPN.

Aug. 25

Warriors agree to deal with Niang

Forward Georges Niang agreed to a one-year, $3.9 million deal with the Golden State Warriors, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Warriors sign guard Williams
Free agent guard Brandon Williams is signing a one-year, $2.6M deal with the Golden State Warriors, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Williams averaged 13 points and 3.9 assists per game last season for the Dallas Mavericks.

Aug. 24

Blazers lose Sharpe to injury
Portland Trail Blazers guard Shaedon Sharpe sustained a torn meniscus in his right knee, and he is expected to miss six months, sources told ESPN.

Sharpe, 23, averaged 20.8 points for the Blazers last season but missed a large chunk of the campaign with a stress fracture of his left fibula.

His four-year, $90 million extension, which he signed last year, officially kicks in this season. Sharpe will make $20.1 million in 2026-27.

Aug. 21

Nuggets signing DeRozan to one-year deal
Six-time NBA All-Star DeMar DeRozan agreed to sign with the Denver Nuggets on a one-year, $3.9 million deal, sources told ESPN on Friday.

DeRozan landed on the Nuggets after speaking to the Miami Heat, Washington Wizards and New Orleans Pelicans during free agency, choosing a significant role in Denver and a chance to compete in the West. The Nuggets' front office and coaches made a strong recruitment effort in recent weeks to secure DeRozan's commitment, showing him how he would complement Nikola Jokic and Jamal Murray as an additional playmaker. He also gives the Nuggets a veteran backcourt presence after sending young, versatile wing Peyton Watson to Cleveland as part of a four-team trade.

Mavs buy out Thompson, to sign with Heat
Klay Thompson is expected to sign with the Miami Heat after clearing waivers following his contract buyout from the Dallas Mavericks, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Friday.

Thompson, 36, was due to make $17.5 million in the final season of his contract with the Mavericks, who announced his buyout Friday afternoon.

He played two seasons for the Mavericks, averaging 12.9 points per game and shooting 38.7% from 3-point range. Thompson passed Damian Lillard last season to rank fourth in career 3-pointers made.

Aug. 20

Harden to return to Cavs
Free agent James Harden agreed to sign a three-year, $97M contract to return to the Cleveland Cavaliers, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania, with a player option for the 2028-29 season.

The Cavs acquired Harden, who turns 37 on Aug. 26, from the LA Clippers in early February in a trade for guard Darius Garland. Cleveland went 21-9 after Harden debuted, tied for the fifth-best record after Feb. 7, as he averaged 20.5 points, 7.7 assists and 4.8 rebounds per game after the All-Star break.

Aug. 19

Watson to Cavs in multiteam trade
The Cleveland Cavaliers, Denver Nuggets and LA Clippers agreed on a trade sending Peyton Watson to the Cavaliers, Max Strus to LA, and an unprotected 2031 Cavs first-round pick and 2032 Sacramento Kings second-rounder to the Nuggets, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. As part of the trade, the Cavaliers will send Tre Mann to the Washington Wizards for Cam Whitmore and a 2027 second-round pick.

Watson will sign a new four-year, $88 million deal with Cleveland.

Aug. 17

Suns, Highsmith agree to one-year deal

The Phoenix Suns and forward Haywood Highsmith agreed to a one-year deal, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Watford, Pelicans agree to one-year deal
Free agent forward Trendon Watford agreed to a one-year, $2.9 million deal with the New Orleans Pelicans, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Watford, 25, considered multiple options, but for New Orleans he serves as a productive two-way get late into the offseason.

Aug. 14

Cavaliers trade Schroder, cash to Hornets for Mann
The Cleveland Cavaliers are trading Dennis Schroder and cash to the Charlotte Hornets for Tre Mann, sources told ESPN on Friday.

The Hornets, Cavaliers and Schroder's rep, Mark Bartelstein of Priority Sports, worked for the past couple months on the deal, which also provides Cleveland flexibility to continue pursuing roster moves and tax savings to keep the team well under the second apron, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

Aug. 13

Beal re-signs with Clippers
Free agent guard Bradley Beal agreed to a two-year, $13.2 million deal to return to the LA Clippers, with a player option in the second season, Mark Bartelstein of Priority Sports told ESPN.

After declining his $5.6 million player option, Beal sifted through options over the last month in free agency, including interest from the Miami Heat, before landing on the Clippers. He returns to LA after rehabbing from hip surgery that cost him all but six games last season.

Aug. 12
Westbrook announces retirement from NBA
Russell Westbrook, the 2017 MVP, a nine-time All-NBA selection and the league's all-time triple-double leader, is retiring from the NBA, the 37-year-old announced on Wednesday. Westbrook had contract offers this offseason from the Sacramento Kings and Washington Wizards but chose to step away on his own terms, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Drafted No. 4 overall by the Seattle SuperSonics in 2008 just before the franchise relocated to Oklahoma City, Westbrook played 11 of his 18 seasons with the Thunder. The electric guard and Hall of Fame lock then spent the remainder of his career with the Houston Rockets, Wizards, Los Angeles Lakers, LA Clippers, Denver Nuggets and Kings.

Westbrook retires with the fifth most assists in NBA history (10,351).

NBA world praises 'legendary' career

Aug. 11

McMenamin: NBA excited to grow product with 3 p.m. opening day tip-off
ESPN's Dave McMenamin went on NBA Today to discuss the recent schedule release for the NBA's opening day and Christmas games.

"I've talked to people around the league today and they're like we could sense the excitement for the NBA right now. So let's experiment with this thing," McMenamin said. "They talked with executives at NBC, and it was kind of a joint decision that this is something we can turn into a celebration of the game. It's already a marquee moment for the league. Let's see if we can enhance it and turn it into a major showcase. Maybe down the line, this becomes a tradition for NBA fans. ... [Also the NBA is] an international game. 3 p.m. Eastern is primetime viewing in Europe."

The Boston Celtics and Detroit Pistons open the season on Tuesday, Oct. 20 at 3 p.m. ET on NBA/Peacock.

What's latest on Kawhi and the Clippers? And updates on Nuggets, Suns
Brian is joined by ESPN's Anthony Slater to discuss the latest in the ongoing Kawhi Leonard-LA Clippers situation, including how it could impact the Toronto Raptors and the Eastern Conference during the 2026-27 season. They move on to the cover the Dillon Brooks' contract and how it impacts the future spending plans for the Phoenix Suns. The duo then closes on how the Denver Nuggets' books put them in trouble moving forward, and a remembrance of Don Nelson.

Windhorst on the newest Kawhi Leonard situation: "That's obviously key: Did he get money from Daktronics? Slater, if this is accurate, the Clippers side of it is devastating.
But let's put that aside for right now. For the actual business of the NBA for the 26-27 season, this is not just a Clipper issue. Last year was a Clipper issue. Now, it is no longer just a Clipper issue. Whether Kahwi Leonard is on the Raptors or not has a huge circumstantial fallout in the Eastern Conference and then obviously like you know DeMar DeRozan is held up to a certain extent, for example. James Harden is hasn't done his business with the Cavs because they're waiting on things.

Latest episodes of the 'Hoop Collective' podcast

Aug. 7

NBA insiders: Updates on the biggest remaining NBA free agents

ESPN's NBA insiders came together to give updates on the top remaining free agents this season. Highlights include:

Multiple teams are pursuing Peyton Watson, including the Atlanta Hawks, LA Clippers, Milwaukee Bucks and Cleveland Cavaliers
The Detroit Pistons remain the favorite to sign Jalen Duren but the two sides are at an impasse
The Los Angeles Lakers are interested Jonathan Kuminga
James Harden is on track for a multi-year deal with Cleveland
DeMar DeRozan has drawn interest from the Miami Heat, Denver Nuggets, Washington Wizards and Cavaliers

Read more: Updates on the biggest remaining NBA free agents

Aug. 5

Brooks, Suns agree to three-year, $73 million extension
Phoenix Suns forward Dillon Brooks agreed Wednesday to a three-year, $73 million contract extension through 2029-30, agent Mike George of Klutch Sports told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Credited with helping to establish a new culture in Phoenix, Brooks is coming off the best season of his nine-year career. He averaged a career-high 20.2 points to go with 3.6 rebounds and 1.8 assists for a surprise 45-win playoff team that maintained continuity throughout the offseason. In addition to bringing back Brooks, the Suns signed Collin Gillespie, Mark Williams and Jordan Goodwin to multiyear contracts and also acquired Miles Bridges and Luke Kennard.

Slater: Kings were actively shopping Sabonis at deadline, draft
ESPN's Anthony Slater reported that the Sacramento Kings were openly shopping forward Domantas Sabonis at the trade deadline and the 2026 draft.

The Kings nearly traded Sabonis to the Toronto Raptors at the deadline in February -- a move he would've welcomed, a source with knowledge of the situation said -- for a package that included RJ Barrett, but the Raptors were unable to get off the three-year, $84 million remaining on Jakob Poeltl's contract, which doomed the deal.
Sabonis had season-ending surgery on a partially torn meniscus later that month, and the Kings revisited trade talks surrounding him this summer. Perry visited with restricted free agent center Jalen Duren in early July and explored the idea of a sign-and-trade swap of big men, but the Detroit Pistons balked at the idea of losing Duren for Sabonis, league sources said.

There were predraft conversations about Sabonis with the Charlotte Hornets (who held pick Nos. 14 and 18) and at least one phone call with the Boston Celtics, team and league sources said, but nothing materialized. In Charlotte's case, the idea would've been to pair Sabonis with point guard LaMelo Ball, but the franchise instead opted to trade Ball for draft picks and lean further into a youth movement.

Why Dolan is so worried about the second apron
The New York Knicks' championship parade has not even started, but there are already questions over whether finances will break up the roster.

"If we could bring back the whole team, exactly as is, why wouldn't you?" Knicks owner James Dolan said Wednesday on WFAN's "Carton Show." "I don't know if we'll be able to.

"We're willing to stretch, but there's certain things in the NBA that you'd have to be suicidal to do. One of them is the second apron. Cannot go into the second apron."

Including the 24th pick in next week's draft (June 23 and 24, 8 p.m. ET on ABC/ESPN), New York is $13 million below the second apron and has decisions with free agents Landry Shamet, Mitchell Robinson and possibly Jose Alvarado. (Alvarado has until Monday to decide on his $4.5 million option.) The entire starting five, meanwhile, is under contract through at least 2026-27. Karl-Anthony Towns is extension-eligible this summer and can become a free agent in the 2027 offseason if an agreement is not reached.

The second apron is a punitive luxury tax threshold restricting how teams add to their rosters in free agency, trades and the draft. In the case of the Knicks, the team would not be allowed to send cash in a trade, use the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception, aggregate salaries in a trade or use more than 100% of the traded player exception.

A team cannot trade its first-round pick seven years out if it finishes over the second apron in consecutive seasons, which no team has ever done. That same pick could be moved back to the end of the first round if a team finishes over the second apron in three out of four seasons. Luckily for Dolan and the Knicks, there are no rules that prohibit a team from retaining its own players.

New York can exceed the threshold to sign Robinson, Shamet and Alvarado. If the Knicks let the three players sign elsewhere, they would have their first-round pick (New York also has the 31st and 55th picks in the second round), the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception and $2.5 million veteran minimum exceptions available as replacements.

Why LaMelo's flagrant 2 falls into a gray area
The NBA retroactively assessed Charlotte Hornets guard LaMelo Ball with a flagrant foul 2 for tripping Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo in Tuesday's Eastern Conference play-in game, which Charlotte won in overtime thanks to Ball's last-second layup.

But for the Heat and their fans, it doesn't erase Adebayo's injury, it doesn't remove Ball from Friday's 8-9 game against the Orlando Magic and it all but certainly won't impact the Hornets should they reach the first round.

That's because one quirk of the tournament's addition is that, not unlike the NBA Cup title game, the play-in tournament lives as its own statistical entity. They are neither playoff nor regular-season games, with no bearing on postseason and regular-season stats or awards.

That's also the case with flagrant foul points, which can have a massive impact when they start to add up. In 2016, Draymond Green was suspended for Game 5 of the NBA Finals for accumulating four flagrant points over the course of the postseason, something that helped Cleveland pull off its stunning 3-1 comeback.

While the Hornets' playoff stay isn't likely to last as long -- Charlotte needs to win Friday just to set up a first-round meeting with the top-seeded Detroit Pistons -- Ball entering the playoffs with two flagrant points would have at least given heft to the belated punishment.

Instead, the decision felt fairly hollow. And in asking sources around the league Wednesday ahead of the NBA's announcement that Ball wouldn't be suspended, opinions were mixed. Some argued that a hefty fine would suffice, because you shouldn't retroactively remove him from the next game because of Adebayo's unfortunate injury. Others argued the opposite, saying he should have to sit out Friday's win-and-in showdown.

None of it, however, will reverse the agonizing end to Miami's season.
